The paper validates both scaled-model measurements and numerical simulations for predicting the bistatic radar cross section (BRCS) of a stealth airborne target.
The stealth target used in the study is called FLAMME, a scaled model of a stealth airborne vehicle.
The numerical simulations use the fast multipole method (FMM) to solve large-scale electromagnetic problems.
The frequency range for both measurements and computations is 2 to 4 GHz.
The numerical simulation involves more than 12,000 unknowns for the three-dimensional electromagnetic problem.
The computational complexity of the FMM is O(N^1.5), where N is the number of unknowns.
The relative RMS error between measured and computed BRCS values for HH polarization at 3 GHz is 2.7 dB.
The agreement between measured and computed BRCS values validates both prediction techniques.
Minor disagreements between measured and computed results are attributed to manufacturing imperfections and measurement artifacts.
Polarimetric calibration is used to convert the measured scattering matrix into the calibrated scattering matrix.
The BRCS matrix is computed by taking the squared magnitude of the elements of the calibrated scattering matrix.
The white areas in the RCS contour plots correspond to values of RCS less than -40 dBm².
The Rao-Wilton-Glisson (RWG) basis functions are used to discretize the target surface into triangular facets.
The FMM reduces both computational complexity and memory requirements.
The study demonstrates the accuracy and efficiency of the FMM for large-scale electromagnetic problems.
The scaled-model measurements are performed at the ONERA facility in France.
The numerical simulations are performed at Bilkent University in Turkey.
The FLAMME model is made of solid conducting material and does not include dielectric or radar absorbing materials.
The shape of the FLAMME is designed to achieve a low monostatic RCS at centimetric wavelengths.
The V shape of the wings allows incident waves to reflect in downward and bistatic directions.
The aft part of the body is jagged to cancel the scattering of surface waves in the monostatic front direction.
The projections of all leading and trailing edges of the wings on a horizontal plane are oriented along only two directions, called the 'dustbin' directions.
The monostatic RCS of the scaled model is concentrated around four directions perpendicular to the two dustbin directions.
The length of the leading edges of the wings is about 45 cm, constituting the dominant mechanisms of scattering from the FLAMME.
The length of the trailing edges of the wings is much shorter, making their scattering contribution secondary.
